You are being evaluated on Continual-ARC, a lifelong stream of ARC-style grid puzzles.
Each puzzle instance has a task id and a test input grid. Tasks recur across the
stream with fresh inputs. Each instance is a separate conversation: the next one
starts without this one's messages.

On every message you must choose exactly one action and put it as a JSON object
on the last line of your reply:
  {"action": "submit", "grid": [[0, 1, 2], [3, 4, 5]]}   submit an output grid
  {"action": "request_demos"}                            ask for one more demonstration pair for this task
  {"action": "finish"}                                   end the instance, once it is over
Grids are lists of rows; cells are integers 0-9; dimensions are 1-30.

Each demo request returns one more input-output pair of the task, up to the demo cap shown
with the input.

Scoring: every wrong submission costs 1 and every demo request costs 1. An
instance is over when a submission is correct or when the attempt cap is reached, and
reaching the cap is charged the full cap. Feedback on a submission is only
correct/incorrect. There is no way to abandon an instance, and finish is refused until
the instance is over. Each instance is scored on its own, and lower cost is better.

How to work, in every instance (follow this exactly): keep a program library in the folder /home/ubuntu/continual-arc-baselines/.workbench/runs/adhoc-openclawlearner-1790687887/attempts/6363bae62cf74cadb6849e205726b671/system/state/workspace/programs, one Python file per task, named for its task id (/home/ubuntu/continual-arc-baselines/.workbench/runs/adhoc-openclawlearner-1790687887/attempts/6363bae62cf74cadb6849e205726b671/system/state/workspace/programs/<task id>.py), defining transform(grid), which takes an input grid as a list of lists of integers and returns the output grid.
1. When an instance starts, look for the task's file. If it exists, run its transform on the test input and submit the result before anything else.
2. If there is no file, or its answer was wrong, request demonstration pairs as you judge necessary, write or fix transform, and run it on every pair you have received until it reproduces all of them; then submit its output for the test input. Checking a program on the pairs is free.
3. Submit only grids that your program produced.
4. After the verdict, save the program that reproduced all the pairs to the task's file, replacing any older version, then finish.

name: continual-arc
description: Solve Continual-ARC puzzles by implementing and validating task-id transforms against demos before submissions.
---

# Continual-ARC instances

1. On every puzzle turn, reply with exactly one supported action JSON object and no surrounding prose or tool narration. Check `programs/<task id>.py`. If present, load it by file path (task IDs may contain hyphens, so do not import using a normalized module name), verify callable `transform(grid)`, and run it on the test input; submit that exact output before editing a valid cache. If missing/malformed, use demonstrations. Use `python3`; verify output values and dimensions rather than reconstructing the answer manually. For transcribed fixture grids, assert stated row count and every row width before interpreting a failed transform; distinguish transcription/runtime failure from evidence against the rule. Keep every grid, demo, and derived output in this instance's conversational state; other instances may reuse the task ID but have distinct inputs, demos, and attempt state.
2. For a new task or unusable cache, infer one coherent rule from all demos and implement it. After each demo, save its exact input/output as a fixture and run one harness that checks the candidate against every accumulated pair, reporting the first differing coordinate as well as shape. Treat exact reproduction of all retained pairs as a hard gate: do not submit a test prediction from an unvalidated candidate, even if its transform runs successfully. If a submission is incorrect, first re-run the exact submitted program and compare it against those fixtures; do not make another guess until its demo mismatches and the alternative rule's differing predictions are explicit. Request another demo only if it can distinguish live hypotheses; requests and wrong submissions cost score. First identify the structural layout from the examples: horizontal/vertical separators, panel boundaries, repeated motif pitch, and the actual coordinates/colors sampled for the output. Reproduce at least two demos with different grid sizes before accepting a coordinate rule; do not infer the output by eyeballing the test alone. Derive color and overlap operations by testing exact demo cells, including background and non-background examples; do not assume a divider or a fixed color mapping generalizes across examples. Treat color 0 as an ordinary color unless the demos establish that it is transparent or background; a template may use zero-valued cells as visible foreground.
3. Before submitting, run the current transform on the test and submit exactly its output. Serialize or copy the program's result directly into the action; do not hand-reconstruct the grid, since a single mistyped row width makes it invalid. After an incorrect verdict, inspect the exact submitted output and source, treat the verdict as counterevidence, and reconsider the whole rule against every demo and test; do not patch guesses or submit unverified output. If the failed candidate came from a cached program and no demos are available, request a demo before editing or trying another prediction; a repeated run or unchanged rewrite of that candidate adds no evidence. After repeated failures, pause before another attempt: state the competing hypotheses, identify evidence in demos that distinguishes them, and test the full candidate against all retained pairs. Treat feedback saying an output is not a valid grid as an output-format/serialization failure first: verify outer type, dimensions, row lengths, and integer range against the stated constraints; do not infer a puzzle-rule failure until those checks pass. If demos leave competing rules, make each candidate predict the complete outputs for every retained pair and compare the cells that differ between hypotheses; spend another demo only when its possible result would choose between them. After the demo cap, if no candidate reproduces all demos, keep the uncertainty explicit and do not turn an unsupported guess into a claimed validated rule; choose another attempt only when the retained evidence supports it. Do not edit the task file to an unvalidated candidate.
4. Once the instance is over (correct verdict or attempt cap), re-run the exact final candidate against every received demo before saving. Save/replace the task file only if that candidate reproduces every demo exactly; otherwise leave the prior file unchanged. A correct test verdict does not establish demo consistency. Then finish only once the instance is over.
